title: The Woman Who Drew the Bathtub
author: Donella H. Meadows
wiifm: Why does a sound business keep overshooting, swinging from too busy to too quiet, hiring in a panic and then cutting in a panic? This is the story of a chemist from Illinois who helped build a computer model of the whole world, was mocked for it, moved to a farm in Vermont, and died before finishing the plain-English book she had always meant to write. Her friends finished it for her. You will come away seeing stocks, flows, delays and feedback loops everywhere, and knowing which levers in your own business actually move anything.

ch.h: A chemist who wanted the whole picture
b: Donella Meadows, known to everyone as Dana, was born on 13 March 1941 in Elgin, Illinois, a manufacturing town on the Fox River west of Chicago. She was clever, curious and practical, and she went to Carleton College in Minnesota to study chemistry, graduating in 1963. From there she went to Harvard, and in 1968 she finished a doctorate in biophysics.

It would have been easy to stay in the laboratory, looking at smaller and smaller pieces of living things. But Dana was more interested in how pieces fit together. With her husband, Dennis Meadows, she had made a long overland journey through Asia, and she had seen poverty, crowded cities and stripped land at close quarters. She came back wanting to understand why well-meaning efforts to fix such things so often made them worse.

The tool she found was being built at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology by an engineer called Jay Forrester. He called it system dynamics. Instead of studying parts, it modelled the way parts feed back on each other over time, using computers to follow loops of cause and effect that the human mind cannot track unaided. Dana joined the team. It was the decision that shaped the rest of her life.
Hold on to that starting point, a biophysicist who distrusted looking at parts. It is the whole book in one sentence: the behaviour of a system cannot be understood by listing what it is made of.
ch.cap: Dana turns from the microscope to Forrester's feedback loops

ch.h: The computer that ruined the party
b: In 1970 a group of industrialists and thinkers called the Club of Rome asked the MIT team a vast question: what happens if the world's population and industry keep growing on a finite planet? Dana, Dennis and their colleagues built a computer model of the world economy called World3, linking population, food, industry, resources and pollution through their feedback loops.

The results were published in March 1972 as a slim book called The Limits to Growth, with Dana as lead author. She was barely thirty. It sold in the millions and was translated into dozens of languages. It also made her, among many economists, a figure of fun.

The attacks had some substance. Economists including William Nordhaus pointed out that the model handled prices and technological substitution crudely: when something becomes scarce, its price rises and people find alternatives, and World3 captured that weakly. But the popular version of the book quickly became something it never was. A set of conditional scenarios, each saying if the world does this, then that tends to follow, was remembered as a prophecy of doom on a fixed date.

That caricature has outlived the argument. Decades later the Australian physicist Graham Turner, first at CSIRO in 2008 and then at the University of Melbourne in 2014, laid thirty years of real data against the original runs and found the world had tracked closest to the scenario the authors called the standard run. That proves less than admirers claim, since a rough model can match reality for years for the wrong reasons. It proves more than the critics would like. Dana learned early how an argument gets remembered, and it made her careful about explaining what a model is.
ch.cap: World3's curves overshoot and fall while economists scoff, 1972

b: After Limits, Dana did not chase fame. She took a teaching post at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, where she taught for nearly thirty years, and she lived on and worked a small farm. She wanted to live inside the kind of system she wrote about, to feel the delays and feedbacks of soil, weather and animals in her own hands.

She also wanted to be understood by ordinary people. From the mid-eighties she wrote a weekly newspaper column called The Global Citizen, explaining environmental and economic questions in plain language to readers who would never open a journal. She was named a Pew Scholar in 1991 and a MacArthur Fellow in 1994.

In 1996 she founded the Sustainability Institute, attached to an organic farm and a cohousing community at Cobb Hill in Hartland, Vermont. And all the while she was drafting the book she had always meant to write: a short primer, almost without mathematics, that would teach anybody to see the world as she saw it.

She never finished it. In February 2001, at fifty-nine, she died suddenly of bacterial meningitis. Her colleague Diana Wright edited the manuscript, and Thinking in Systems appeared in 2008. It is about two hundred and twenty pages long, and for anyone running a business it may be the most useful book in this whole week.
ch.cap: Dana carries a pail across her farm at dusk

b: Dana begins where she began with her students: with a bathtub. A stock is anything that accumulates, something you could in principle photograph at a moment. Water in the tub, money in the bank, staff on the payroll, trust between two people, goodwill in a market. A flow is the rate at which the stock fills or drains: litres per minute, revenue per month, hires and resignations.

Three lessons follow, and all three are routinely ignored. First, stocks change slowly even when flows change instantly. You can turn off the tap this second and the tub is still full. You can cut spending today and your cash will take months to recover. You can start being honest with a client this afternoon, and trust will refill at its own pace however sincere you are. The commonest failure of nerve in business is abandoning a correct change because the stock has not yet moved.

Second, stocks are buffers, and buffers let a system survive shocks. Three months of cash absorbs a bad quarter. Three days does not. The catch is that buffers cost money, so there is constant pressure to trim them, and the trimming looks like efficiency right up to the day it looks like insolvency.

Third, and most subtly, a stock lets the inflow and outflow run at different speeds. Because there is water in the tub, the tap and the drain do not have to match. Because there is stock in the warehouse, the factory and the customer do not have to move in lockstep. Every buffer in your business is bought independence.
ch.cap: A bathtub fills and drains: Dana's first lesson in stocks

b: Stocks and flows on their own are plumbing. What makes a system come alive is feedback, when the level of a stock changes the flows that fill or drain it. Dana insisted there are only two kinds.

A balancing loop seeks a goal and corrects itself. A thermostat is the classic case: the room cools, the heating comes on, the room warms, the heating goes off. A market where high prices draw in more supply, which brings prices down, is another. Balancing loops bring stability, and they are also why systems resist you. Push against a goal-seeking loop and it pushes back.

A reinforcing loop amplifies. The more you have, the more you get: compound interest, word of mouth, a reputation that brings opportunities that build the reputation, debt that breeds interest that breeds more debt. Growth and collapse are the same reinforcing loop running in opposite directions.

Almost everything interesting is a handful of these loops competing, with first one and then another taking charge. A young company is a reinforcing loop outrunning the balancing ones; a mature company is the balancing loops catching up. So when something baffles you, Dana says, do not list its parts. Ask which loop is in charge right now, and what would have to change for another to take over.
ch.cap: Thermostat balances while a snowball reinforces down the slope

ch.h: The hotel shower and the car dealer
b: Now add time. Everybody has stood in an unfamiliar hotel shower, turned the tap, felt nothing, turned it further, and further again, until scalding water arrives and you wrench it back the other way and find yourself under ice. You blame yourself or the hotel. In fact you have just shown the most important thing about any system: when there is a delay between action and feedback, aggressive correction produces oscillation.

Dana's set piece is a car dealer who likes to keep about ten days of stock on the forecourt. Sales step up once and stay up. Sensibly, he does not react to a single good day but averages sales over several days, which is a delay in seeing. Then he orders, and the cars take weeks to arrive, which is a delay in response. All the while he is short, so he orders hard to catch up. Then everything lands together, the forecourt overflows, he stops ordering, and the same delays leave him short again.
The dealership now swings back and forth for good around a demand that changed only once. The owner is not foolish. Every one of his rules makes sense. The swings are manufactured by the delays.

Her counter-intuitive fix is to respond less violently. Order a smaller share of the gap each time, and the swings die away. Where you cannot shorten a delay, soften the response. In practice, write down for each number you steer by how long before you can see a real change and how long before your action bites. A hire takes months to find and months more to become productive. Then make small corrections on a fixed timetable and hold them for a full delay before judging. Experienced operators often look lazy for exactly this reason. They have learned not to yank the tap.
ch.cap: Scalding then icy shower; a car lot swamped by orders

b: From the economist Herbert Simon, Dana took the idea of bounded rationality. Everyone acts sensibly on the information available from where they sit, and nobody sits where they can see everything. The fisherman sees his catch, not the fish stock. The manager sees the report, not the customer. The customer sees the price, not the cost.

The consequence is a blunt instruction: stop explaining bad outcomes by bad people. Put someone else in the same chair, with the same information and the same incentives, and they will mostly do the same thing. Her test is whether you can describe the behaviour you dislike as a reasonable response to the view from that chair. If you can, you have found a system to redesign, not a person to replace.

She also catalogued the traps that sensible people build together. Drift to low performance, where each bad period lowers the target and so licenses the next; the cure is to anchor standards to your best ever, never to last quarter. Escalation, as in price wars, which ends only when one side refuses to compete on that axis. Success to the successful, where the winners get the resources that make them win again, so the best leads always go to the salesperson who already has the best leads. The tragedy of the commons, where nobody feels the cost of overusing what is shared.

And the most personal one, shifting the burden to the intervenor. A rescuer relieves the symptom, the system's own ability withers, and more rescue is needed. The founder who personally saves every deal guarantees that nobody else ever learns to close one.
ch.cap: A fisherman hauls his catch above an emptying sea

b: Her most famous piece of writing began in irritation. In the mid-nineties Dana sat in a meeting about the new rules for global trade, full of serious people enthusiastic about growth. She grew so exasperated that she got up, went to the flip chart, and wrote a list of all the places you can intervene in a system, from the weakest to the strongest. Polished up and published as Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System, it is probably the most widely shared thing she wrote.

At the bottom, at number twelve, are numbers: taxes, subsidies, targets, the parameters everyone argues about. Above them come the size of buffers, the physical layout of stocks and flows, the length of delays, and the strength of balancing and reinforcing loops. At number six come information flows, who knows what and when. Then rules, the power of a system to reorganise itself, its goals, its paradigm or unspoken assumptions, and at the top the ability to hold no model as final.

Two lessons sit inside the list. Almost all management effort goes to number twelve, because numbers are easy to change, which is precisely why changing them so rarely does much. And the higher you go, the less tangible and often the cheaper the lever becomes.

She called the list a work in progress, and later researchers have noted that the exact ordering was never tested; Abson and colleagues in 2017 found the deep levers really are neglected but that hard evidence for the precise ranking is thin. Treat it as a superb checklist that stops you reaching for the obvious lever, not as a measured scale.
ch.cap: Exasperated, Dana writes the leverage points on a flip chart

b: Dana's favourite proof that information flows are underused came from a housing development near Amsterdam. The houses were essentially identical, built to the same plan at the same time. But for accidental reasons some had the electricity meter in the basement and some had it in the front hall, where you walked past it every day.

The households with the meter in the hall, she reported, used about a third less electricity. Same houses, same prices, same appliances. The only difference was that one group could see the dial spinning as they lived, and the other had to go downstairs to look.

No tax, no campaign, no appeal to conscience. Just the consequence made visible to the person causing it, at the moment they caused it. That is why information sits six places above fiddling with prices.

In a business, take whatever behaviour annoys you most: invoices left unchased, quotes going out late, problems hidden until too late. You have probably been attacking it with a target or a bonus, at level twelve. Climb instead. A single shared board showing the age of unpaid invoices by owner will beat any amount of nagging. Then look at the rules: if salespeople are paid on bookings, you are buying bookings, not cash.
ch.cap: Twin houses: the visible hall meter saves a third

b: Dana did not live to see the primer published, but she left its spirit in her last essays. Systems thinking, she wrote, is less a toolkit than a practice. The world will keep surprising you, because everything you know, and everything anyone knows, is only a model. The right response is not to stop modelling but to hold your models lightly, test them against what happens, and stay a learner.

That humility links her to the rest of this week. Yesterday Taleb told you to expect the shock. Dana shows you where shocks are made: not mostly outside, but inside, by perfectly ordinary parts connected by delays and loops nobody drew. The slow quarter you blame on the market may be the result of the marketing you cut nine months earlier.

So the life story gives you a working method. Find your stocks and protect your buffers. Name the loop that is in charge. Write down your delays and soften your corrections. Assume the people in your system are being sensible from where they sit. And when something annoys you, reach past the numbers for the information, the rules and the goals.

A chemist from Elgin built a model of the whole world and was laughed at for it. Then she went home to a farm and wrote, in the plainest English she could manage, how to see the machinery underneath everything. Her friends finished the book. It has been teaching people to stop yanking the tap ever since.
ch.cap: A colleague finishes Dana's unfinished primer by lamplight

take: Judge the flow, not the stock
Stocks like cash and trust respond slowly. If the flow has changed in the right direction, hold your nerve rather than abandoning a sound decision too early.
Cash reserves, spare stock and slack let one part of the business absorb a shock without passing it on. Trimming them always looks efficient until it is fatal.
Ask whether a balancing loop is resisting you or a reinforcing loop is running away. Diagnosing by loop makes baffling behaviour make sense.
Delay plus aggressive correction equals oscillation. Write down how long each key number takes to show a change, then correct in small steps and wait a full delay.
Blame the chair, not the person
If a behaviour is a rational response to someone's information and incentives, change the system, because a replacement would do the same.
Targets and bonuses are the weakest lever. Making a consequence visible to the person who causes it, as it happens, is cheap and far stronger.
Drift to low performance happens when the target follows last quarter. Set standards from your best ever performance or someone else's.
If you personally fix every crisis, nobody else learns. Invest in others' ability and accept a rough patch while it grows.
recall: What did The Limits to Growth actually claim, and what did Graham Turner's later work show?

It offered conditional scenarios, not a forecast of doom on a date. Turner's comparisons in 2008 and 2014 found real data tracked closest to the standard run, which is interesting but does not prove the model's mechanisms were right.
Why does a stock make a complex system possible?

A stock lets inflow and outflow run at different rates, so the tap and drain, or factory and customer, need not be synchronised. That is why buffers are bought independence, and why removing them passes every shock straight through.
How does the car dealer end up oscillating when demand rose only once?

A delay in seeing sales and a delay in deliveries mean he stays short, over-orders, then gets everything at once and stops ordering, before falling short again. The fix is to correct a smaller share of the gap each time.
What is shifting the burden to the intervenor?
An outside rescuer relieves a symptom while the system's own capacity withers, so more rescue is needed each time. The escape is to build the system's capacity and tolerate a worse patch meanwhile.
Where do numbers and information flows sit among the leverage points, and why does it matter?

Numbers are twelfth, the weakest; information flows are sixth. Most effort goes on numbers because they are easy to change, while making information visible is often free and far more powerful, as the Amsterdam meters showed.
note: Biographical details are from the Donella Meadows Project and published obituaries. Graham Turner's 2008 paper was published through CSIRO and his 2014 update through the University of Melbourne. The Amsterdam meter story is as Meadows reported it and its original study is not well documented. The ranking of leverage points was never empirically derived, as Meadows herself acknowledged; Abson and colleagues (2017) discuss the evidence.
words: The tendency of a system to hold itself steady around a set point by correcting any drift.
Meadows's balancing loops, like a thermostat or a market where high prices draw in supply, are homeostasis at work, and they are why systems push back when you push them.
A regular swinging back and forth either side of a level.
Her car dealer falls into endless oscillation, over-ordering and then under-ordering, around a demand that changed only once, purely because of delays.
Arising from inside a system rather than being imposed from outside.
Meadows argues that most of a business's swings are endogenous, made by its own delays and loops, so the slow quarter blamed on the market may come from marketing cut nine months earlier.
Choosing the first option that is good enough on the information available, rather than searching for the best.
Herbert Simon coined the term alongside bounded rationality, the idea Meadows used to show that people behave sensibly from the limited view of their own chair.
The set of unspoken assumptions that shapes how a whole group sees a problem.
In her list of leverage points, changing a system's paradigm sits near the very top, far above the numbers and targets where most management effort goes.
stories: Dana Meadows loved this one. In a housing development near Amsterdam, the houses were essentially identical: same plan, same builder, same appliances. But for accidental reasons, some had the electricity meter down in the basement and some had it in the front hall, where the family walked past the spinning dial every day. The households with the meter in the hall, she reported, used about a third less electricity. No tax, no campaign, no lecture. Just the consequence made visible to the person causing it, at the moment they caused it. The original study is poorly documented, so tell it as her story, but the lesson has held up well.
The woman at the flip chart

In the mid-nineties Meadows sat in a meeting about new rules for global trade, surrounded by serious people excited about growth. She grew so exasperated that she got up, walked to the flip chart, and wrote out every place you can intervene in a system, from weakest to strongest. At the bottom were numbers: taxes, targets and subsidies, the things everyone argues about. Far above them were information flows, rules, goals and the paradigm itself. Polished up as Leverage Points, it became probably the most widely shared thing she ever wrote. The irony is that almost all management effort still goes to the bottom of her list.

In 1972, barely thirty, Meadows was lead author of The Limits to Growth, a computer model asking what happens if population and industry keep growing on a finite planet. It sold in the millions and made her a figure of fun. Economists such as William Nordhaus fairly said it handled prices crudely, but the public remembered conditional scenarios as a prophecy of doom on a fixed date. Then the Australian physicist Graham Turner, in 2008 and again in 2014, laid thirty years of real data against the original runs. The world had tracked closest to the standard run. That does not prove the model right, but it was not the joke people thought.
biz: Paid search for secured loans is a hotel shower. A click today may become an application weeks later and a completion weeks after that, once the lender has valued the property. Judge budgets on yesterday's leads and you will oscillate like the car dealer. This week, write down the real delays: click to enquiry, enquiry to application, application to completion, by channel. Then set a rule: budget changes happen on a fixed day each week, move by a small share at a time, and are held for one full delay before being judged. Measure cost per completed case on a rolling basis, not cost per lead yesterday.
Put the meter in the hall

In debt advice, the costly failures are often slow ones: a frightened client's WhatsApp message left unanswered for a day, or a vulnerability flag that nobody follows up. A target on conversions sits at the bottom of Meadows's list and can push people towards pressure, which Consumer Duty forbids. Climb to information instead. Put up one shared board showing every open enquiry by owner and how long it has waited, with vulnerable clients highlighted. Track median first-response time and the number of flagged cases chased within a set time. Then check the rules: if anyone is paid only on sign-ups, you are buying sign-ups, not good outcomes.
connects: Adam Smith's account of prices drawing in supply until shortages disappear is one of Meadows's balancing feedback loops, described two centuries before system dynamics.
Boyd's loop of observing, orienting, deciding and acting is a theory of winning through feedback speed, the mirror of Meadows's warning that delays turn sensible decisions into oscillation.
Perrow's tight coupling is what Meadows calls a system without buffers, where a shock passes straight through because there is no stock to absorb it.
recap:
Donella Meadows, known to everyone as Dana, was born in Elgin, Illinois, in nineteen forty-one. She trained as a chemist and took a Harvard doctorate in biophysics, but after a long overland journey through Asia she wanted to understand something bigger: why do well-meaning efforts to fix the world so often make it worse? She found her answer at MIT, in Jay Forrester's system dynamics, which studies not the parts of a thing but the way they feed back on each other over time.

At barely thirty she was lead author of The Limits to Growth, a computer model of the whole world economy published in nineteen seventy-two. It sold in the millions and made her a figure of fun among economists, who were partly right that it handled prices crudely. But it offered scenarios, not a date for doom, and decades later an Australian physicist found that real data had tracked its standard run surprisingly closely. Dana went on to teach at Dartmouth, worked a small farm, wrote a plain English newspaper column, and drafted a primer for ordinary readers. She died suddenly in two thousand and one, at fifty-nine. Her colleague Diana Wright finished the book.

It begins with a bathtub. A stock is anything that accumulates, such as cash, staff or trust, and a flow is whatever fills or drains it. Stocks change slowly even when flows change instantly, so never abandon a good decision just because the stock has not moved yet. And buffers, like cash in the bank, are bought independence.

Next come feedback loops. Balancing loops seek a goal and push back when you push them. Reinforcing loops amplify, which is how both growth and collapse happen. When something baffles you, ask which loop is in charge right now.

Then add delay. Think of a hotel shower, scalding then freezing, or her car dealer, who over-orders, then under-orders, and swings for ever around a demand that changed only once. The cure is gentler correction, held for a full delay before you judge it.

She also taught that people act sensibly from where they sit, so change the chair rather than blaming the person. And her famous list of leverage points warns that numbers and targets, where managers spend most of their effort, are the weakest levers of all. Information is far stronger. In one Dutch housing estate, she reported, homes with the electricity meter in the front hall used about a third less power than identical homes with the meter in the basement.

The line to remember: behaviour comes from structure, so if you want different results, redraw the plumbing.
